nameStory: The dog-rose gets its peculiar name from ancient beliefs that its roots could cure rabid dog bites, though this folk remedy was sadly ineffective. Some say it's called 'dog' rose because it was considered inferior to cultivated garden roses, like calling something a 'dog's dinner.' The scientific name 'canina' literally means 'of the dog' in Latin, cementing this canine connection in botanical history.
description: Dog-rose is a vigorous climbing wild rose that scrambles through hedgerows and forest edges with long, arching canes armed with fierce thorns. This European native can reach 6-10 feet tall, forming dense thickets as it spreads. Its delicate pink or white flowers bloom in early summer, followed by bright red oval fruits called rose hips that persist into winter. Though not originally from New England, it has naturalized in scattered locations across the region.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five delicate petals, usually pale pink or white, about 2 inches across with a sweet, light fragrance. Flowers appear singly or in small clusters of 2-4 blooms from May through July.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 5-7 oval leaflets that feel smooth and have finely toothed edges. The leaflets are arranged along a stem with no fuzzy coating, giving them a clean, bright green appearance.

idTips.label: Thorns
idTips.description: Large, curved thorns shaped like cat claws that hook backward along the stems. These thorns are much more substantial than prickles, with a broad base that's firmly attached to the woody stem.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red, oval-shaped rose hips about 3/4 inch long that turn deep red in fall. They feel firm and smooth, containing several hard, hairy seeds inside the fleshy exterior.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Long, arching canes that climb and scramble through other vegetation, often forming dense tangles. The stems are green when young, becoming brown and woody with age.

habitat: Look for dog-rose along woodland edges, old farm sites, and disturbed areas where it can climb through existing vegetation. It prefers well-drained soils and partial sun, often establishing near old homesteads or in areas with European settlement history. In New England, it's most commonly found in southern regions and is much less common than our native wild roses.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in May, followed quickly by flower buds that swell at branch tips.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in June and July with fragrant pink or white flowers. Spent flowers begin developing into small green fruits.
seasonality.fall: Rose hips ripen to brilliant red-orange and become very prominent as leaves turn yellow and drop.
seasonality.winter: Bare thorny canes remain visible with bright red hips persisting through much of winter, providing food for birds.

funFact: Dog-rose hips contain more vitamin C than oranges and were collected by the millions during World War II in Britain to make syrup when citrus fruits were scarce, helping prevent scurvy in children during the war.
confusionNotes: Dog-rose is easily confused with multiflora rose, but dog-rose has larger, more substantial thorns and lacks the fringed stipules (small leaf-like structures at the base of leaf stems) that multiflora rose displays. Remember: dog-rose thorns are big and curved like dog claws, while multiflora rose has smaller, straighter prickles.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'wild' rose, dog-rose is actually non-native to New England, having escaped from early European settlements. It's much less aggressive than the invasive multiflora rose and is considered relatively benign in our regional ecosystems.
compareHints: Among New England's roses, dog-rose stands out for its large, curved thorns and smooth leaflets without fuzzy coating. Native swamp rose and Carolina rose have straighter thorns and often grow in wetter spots, while invasive multiflora rose has clusters of small white flowers and distinctive fringed stipules that dog-rose lacks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England roses, multiflora rose is unique for its enormous flower clusters (other roses have flowers in smaller groups or singly) and those telltale fringed stipules.
Rugosa rose stands apart from other New England roses with its unmistakable wrinkled leaves - no other rose species has this corrugated texture.

Among New England's wild roses, swamp rose is unique in its preference for wet habitats - while Carolina rose and Virginia rose stick to drier areas, and multiflora rose (an invasive) has much denser thorns and forms larger, more aggressive colonies.
Among New England's wild roses, Carolina rose is the champion spreader, forming low colonies while relatives like swamp rose grow taller and more upright.
Among New England's wild roses, Virginian rose stands out for its glossy leaflets (rugosa rose has wrinkled leaves) and typically 7-9 leaflets per leaf (most others have fewer).

Among New England's roses, Sherard's downy-rose stands out for its compact size and distinctly grayish, downy leaves - most other wild roses like swamp rose or Carolina rose have greener, smoother foliage.

Among New England's wild roses, smooth rose is unique for its nearly thornless stems – multiflora rose has curved thorns, rugosa rose has dense straight prickles, and swamp rose has scattered thorns along its stems.
Memorial rose is unique among New England roses for its prostrate, ground-hugging growth habit - all other rose species in the region grow as upright shrubs.
Among New England's wild roses, shining rose is uniquely low-growing and has by far the glossiest leaves.
Unlike the common multiflora rose with its clusters of small white flowers, cinnamon rose has larger, solitary pink blooms.
Among New England's wild roses, prickly wild rose stands out for its extreme thorniness — it has far more prickles per inch than rugosa rose, swamp rose, or any of our other native roses.
Among New England's roses, sweet-brier is the only one with apple-scented leaves - this fragrance alone separates it from multiflora rose, rugosa rose, and native species.
Climbing prairie rose stands out from other New England roses primarily by its vigorous climbing habit with long, flexible canes.
Unlike New England's native roses such as swamp rose or Carolina rose which have green leaves, red-leaved rose's blue-gray to purplish foliage is unmistakable.
